topic_summary: Analysis of Alberta separatism as a political movement advocating provincial independence from Canada. The movement frames independence as a mechanism to retain resource revenues, escape federal fiscal transfers and climate policy, and maximize hydrocarbon extraction autonomy. Core tension: provincial resource sovereignty vs federal constitutional authority.

key_entities: Canadian federal government (constitutional authority, transfer administrator)
Separatist movements (Wildrose Independence Party, Alberta Prosperity Project)
Hydrocarbon sector (oil sands, natural gas industry)
Equalization transfer system (federal fiscal redistribution mechanism)
Indigenous nations (treaty holders with Crown obligations)
key_tensions: Provincial resource control vs federal environmental/climate authority
Net fiscal contributor status vs equalization payment obligations
Territorial sovereignty claims vs constitutional indivisibility doctrine

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The legitimacy boundary of provincial autonomy within Canadian federalism — what powers provinces hold as inherent vs delegated, and whether resource sovereignty permits unilateral exit
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Constitutional text (BNA Act 1867, Constitution Act 1982) interpreted by Supreme Court of Canada; federal government claims final authority on territorial integrity; separatists claim inherent provincial sovereignty

readings.commitment: Provinces are creatures of federal constitution; no inherent sovereignty; exit requires federal consent
readings.authority_grounding: Supreme Court Reference re Secession of Quebec (1998); constitutional supremacy doctrine
readings.expected_structural_delta: Federal veto over exit; equalization and climate policy are legitimate federal authority; separatism is constitutional nullity

readings.commitment: Confederation was a compact among sovereign provinces; provinces retain residual sovereignty; exit negotiable under duress
readings.authority_grounding: Compact theory of Confederation; provincial rights tradition; Quebec sovereignty movement precedent
readings.expected_structural_delta: Federal authority conditional on provincial consent; equalization negotiable; climate policy subject to provincial override; exit requires negotiation not permission

readings.commitment: Provincial ownership of natural resources (s.92A Constitution Act 1982) grounds absolute sovereignty; resource control = territorial sovereignty
readings.authority_grounding: Natural resource amendment (1982); property rights absolutism; libertarian sovereignty theory
readings.expected_structural_delta: Resource jurisdiction = full sovereignty; federal climate/fiscal policy is illegitimate extraction; unilateral exit is constitutional right

axiom_contradictions.basis: Constitutional subordination holds that provinces have no sovereignty independent of federal grant; resource sovereignty primacy holds that resource ownership grounds inherent sovereignty. No framework can hold both: either sovereignty derives from constitution (subordination) or from property (primacy).

Constitutional subordination holds provinces are created by and subordinate to federal authority; compact federalism holds provinces pre-existed and delegated limited powers upward. No framework can hold both: either provinces are creatures of federation or federation is creature of provinces.

omegas.description: Does an independent Alberta maintain Crown treaty obligations with Indigenous nations? If not, the sovereignty kernel becomes a Snare for treaty holders. If yes, resource sovereignty is constrained by prior commitments.
omegas.source: Deferred axis indigenous_treaty_collision + Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory)

omegas.description: Would an independent Alberta achieve international recognition without federal consent? Unilateral declaration may produce a non-recognized state with limited treaty/trade capacity.
Is hydrocarbon_lock_in a true Mountain (geology + sunk infrastructure) or a Piton of policy choice? Global energy transition and stranded asset risk may reclassify.
Compact federalism reading relies on contested historical interpretation. Supreme Court rejected compact theory in 1998 Quebec reference. Is this reading legally viable or politically aspirational?
Who benefits from separatism_as_arbitrage? Separatist leadership clearly benefits. Does the median Albertan benefit, or only high-income resource sector workers? Distributional analysis missing.
